notes.meaning: David fled to the town of Nob, where the priests lived and where the sacred tent of worship was set up. Ahimelech the priest trembled with fear when he saw David arriving without an escort. He was worried that something was wrong between David and King Saul.

David told Ahimelech that Saul had sent him on a secret mission and that his men were told to meet him elsewhere. This was not true, but David lied because he was terrified for his life. His deceit later brought terrible harm to the priests when Saul found out.

David asked the priest for whatever food was on hand, requesting five loaves of bread. He needed food immediately to feed himself and his traveling companions. Even God's chosen leaders face times of deep physical hunger and need.

Ahimelech explained that he had no ordinary bread, but only the holy bread from the sacred table. This consecrated bread was normally meant only for priests. However, the priest was willing to share it if David and his men were ceremonially clean and had abstained from sexual relations.

David reassured Ahimelech that his men had stayed away from women during their journey. He explained that their bodies and gear were kept clean even on ordinary trips, so they were certainly pure now. The priest could rest assured that the bread would not be defiled.

The priest gave David the holy bread because there was nothing else to eat. These loaves had just been taken off the table before the Lord on the Sabbath to make room for fresh warm bread. Jesus later pointed to this event to teach that God values human life and mercy over strict ritual rules.

Saul's chief herdsman, an Edomite named Doeg, happened to be at the sanctuary that day. He was staying there before the Lord, likely keeping a religious vow or resting for the Sabbath. His presence was an ominous sign that David's visit would soon be reported to Saul.

David asked Ahimelech if there was a spear or a sword available for him to take. He claimed he had left home without any weapons because the king's business was so urgent. David was still keeping up his false story to hide his desperate flight.

The priest offered David the sword of Goliath, which had been wrapped in a cloth behind the priestly vestment as a trophy of God's victory. David gladly accepted it, declaring that no other weapon could compare. Holding it served as a powerful reminder of how the Lord had saved him in the past.

David fled from the land of Israel that very day to escape Saul and sought refuge with Achish, the king of Gath. Going to a Philistine city was a dangerous move because Gath was Goliath's hometown. David's fear drove him to take extreme risks in hope of finding safety.

The officers of King Achish quickly recognized David and spoke to their king about him. They called him the king of the land and repeated the popular victory song about his military triumphs over the Philistines. David's fame had spread far beyond Israel's borders, putting him in grave danger.

David heard what the Philistine officials were saying and took their words seriously. He realized they saw him as a deadly enemy and became terrified of King Achish. His fear reminded him that relying on foreign rulers could not give true safety.

To save his life, David pretended to be completely out of his mind. He made scratches and marks on the city gates and let saliva run down into his beard. By acting like a helpless madman, he hoped the Philistines would pity him rather than kill him.

King Achish saw David's strange behavior and rebuked his servants for bringing him into his presence. He declared that the man was clearly insane and questioned why they had brought him at all. David's act worked, convincing the king that he was harmless.

Achish asked sarcastically if he was short of madmen, refusing to let such a person enter his royal palace. He drove David away, allowing him to escape harm. Even through this humiliating moment, God preserved David's life so he could flee back to safety.
